newsitem.title: UK: IPE Brent closes down on bearish API forecasts.
newsitem.headline: IPE Brent closes down on bearish API forecasts.

text.p: IPE Brent crude futures closed down on Tuesday, having tracked a slide in NYMEX heating oil which in turn came under pressure from expectations of bearish weekly stock data to be released after the close of trade tonight.
"It's looking like the APIs are going to show a (distillate) build on the year...It's pulling everything else down," said one broker.
March Brent closed nine cents lower at $22.45 a barrel, off the session low of $22.30.
After opening stronger, NYMEX March heating oil made a push for the upside but quickly shed gains and closed over one cent a gallon lower.

Market-watchers said that while this evening's oil inventory report from the American Petroleum Institute (API) is expected to show in draw on distillate stocks last week, it could show a year-on-year surplus for the first time in more than a year.
Dealers are expecting a draw of around 2.6 million barrels for the week ended January 31.

"Distillate stocks relative to year-ago are worth watching - if the current deficit turns into a surplus there could be a negative psychological impact on the market," GNI's Leslie Nicholas said in a daily report.
U.S. crude stocks are expected to grow between two and three million barrels due to steady imports and cuts in refinery throughputs due to maintenance.
The API data is also expected to show a two to three million barrel rise in gasoline stocks.
Feb gas oil closed $1 down at $203 a tonne, $1 up from the intra-day low, but more than $5 off the session high. The March Brent/gas oil crack spread ended at $3.67 a barrel.

Earlier, a report that United Nations inspectors have discovered that Iraq has continued to develop missiles in contravention of U.N. resolutions sparked a short-lived jump on both Brent and gas oil futures.
In an advance release from Wednesday's edition, the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) said the United States could make a decision this week on whether to launch a missile strike at Iraq.
Later, the U.S. State Department said there was no "heightened concern" about Iraq, but it declined to comment on the newspaper report.
